_notes: The bishop leans on his pastors. Requests are common and leave a way to say no that costs something; demands are rare (low baseWeight, a particular temper) and say plainly that they are not requests. Church changes here go through decor effects, so the reaction is authored, not computed. Flags: bp_kept_orientem, bp_early_mass_orientem, bp_rail_kept, bp_rail_standing, bp_tabernacle_letter, bp_grant_split, bp_ordinary_in_latin, bp_latin_weekday, bp_renewal_taken, bp_renewal_roof, bp_room_promised, bp_complied_demand, bp_defied_bishop, bp_tlm_wind_down, bp_appealed_rome, bp_drafts_to_bishop, bp_did_favor, bp_asked_for_parish, bp_housed_brother, bp_housed_with_conditions.

events.title: A Word After Confirmations
events.body: {@bishop} confirms forty-one of your teenagers on a Tuesday evening and stays for the reception, which he does not always do. He is gracious with the parents and photographs badly and eats one cookie. When the hall has thinned he asks whether you would walk him to the car, and in the parking lot, with the driver already at the wheel, he says the thing he came to say. He was in the church for an hour. He noticed which way the altar is used. He does not say it is wrong, because it is not, and he knows the rubrics as well as you do. He says the diocese has a way of doing things, and a pastor who does something else is telling his people something about the diocese whether he means to or not. He would be grateful if you would think about it. He says grateful twice. Then he gets in the car. The driver, who has heard all of it, looks at you with something that might be sympathy.
events.flavorPrompt: A parking-lot conversation after a reception. Cordial, brief, and not a request in the ordinary sense.

choices.label: Turn the altar back to the people before the month is out
choices.outcome: You tell the sacristan on Thursday and the choir on Friday and the parish on Sunday, in a paragraph that says nothing about the bishop. The families who drove in for the seven o'clock understand it anyway. The chancery hears within the week, as it hears everything, and this time what it hears is good.

choices.label: Write to him: the rubrics permit it, the parish asked for it, and you will keep it
choices.outcome: The letter is two pages and every sentence in it is true. He does not answer it. Three weeks later the vicar for clergy mentions, in the middle of something else, that the bishop read it. He does not say how it went. You have kept the altar and spent something you cannot see.

choices.label: Turn the main Mass back and keep the seven o'clock as it is
choices.outcome: The ten-thirty faces the people again. The seven o'clock, which was always the Mass for the people who wanted it, keeps its direction, and you do not put that in the bulletin. It is the sort of arrangement a bishop can decide not to know about, and this one decides not to.

events.title: The Rail
events.body: The letter comes on chancery paper but it is plainly from him: the sentences are too short for the chancellor. He writes that he was glad to see the church full at the anniversary Mass. He writes that the altar rail is handsome. He writes that a rail is also a line, and that he has spent his episcopate trying to take lines out of churches, and that he would not ask a pastor to take out something the parish paid for, but that he would be glad to hear it was being considered. He writes that he is aware some of the people kneel at it, and that he is aware that is their right. He closes with the assurance of his prayers, which is the phrase bishops use when they are done. There is no deadline in the letter and no consequence, and that is the point of it. What he wants is for you to know what he wants.
events.flavorPrompt: A short letter from a bishop who dislikes lines. Courteous, without a threat, unmistakable.

choices.label: Take the rail out, and pay a carpenter to do it gently
choices.outcome: The carpenter takes two days and leaves the marble in the basement where the last pastor found it. Three families write. One of them writes to the bishop, which is how the bishop learns that you did what he asked, and how you learn that he learned it.

choices.label: Leave it, and do not answer the letter
choices.outcome: You file the letter. Nothing happens, which is what happens with most letters, and then in the spring the vicar general asks, in passing, about the rail. You say it is being considered. He writes that down.

effects.value: The bishop asked about the rail and was not answered

choices.label: Keep the rail and ask the people to receive standing at it
choices.outcome: You announce it as a practical matter, which nobody believes. The kneelers kneel anyway, because they are kneelers, and you do not stop them, and the bishop, when he hears, hears that you tried. It is the kind of half measure that satisfies no one and keeps the peace.

events.title: Where He Is Kept
events.body: {@bishop} says Mass at {parish} for the feast of the patron and afterward, vested still, walks the length of the church looking for the tabernacle. He finds it in the chapel of reservation, where the last renovation put it, behind a door with its own lamp. He stands there a while. At lunch he says that he has always thought a person walking into a church should be able to find the Lord without asking, and that he understands why the chapel was built, and that he does not agree with it. He says he would be glad to come back and bless the tabernacle in the sanctuary, if it were moved. He says it would mean a great deal to him. He does not say what it would mean to you if it were not moved, and you understand that he does not have to.
events.flavorPrompt: A bishop finding the tabernacle in a side chapel and saying, over lunch, what he thinks of that.

choices.label: Move it back to the center, and invite him to bless it
choices.outcome: The mason takes a week and the bishop comes back in Advent and blesses it with the whole parish watching. The people who built the chapel of reservation sit in the back and say nothing. Some of them do not come back.

choices.label: Explain the chapel: adoration all day, a door that locks, a parish that uses it
choices.outcome: You tell him about the eight-to-eight adoration schedule and the widows who keep it and the fact that the church itself cannot be left open in this neighborhood. He listens. He says he had not known about the schedule. He does not say he was wrong, and he does not come back in Advent.

choices.label: Ask him to put it in writing, so the parish council hears it from him
choices.outcome: He looks at you for a moment and says of course. The letter comes, and it is careful, and it is his, and when you read it to the council they hear a bishop asking rather than a pastor deciding. They agree to move it within the year. He notes that you needed the letter.

events.title: A Grant With a Purpose
events.body: The finance officer calls to say the diocese has money for you, which has never happened before, and then explains the money. {@bishop} has set aside a fund, from a bequest, for what the letter calls the restoration of sacred furnishings in parish churches. Your parish has been identified. The grant is nine thousand dollars. It is restricted, and what it is restricted to is an altar rail, and the finance officer says this without any tone at all, the way he says everything. There is a form. There is a deadline. Nobody has said that a pastor who declines the bishop's money for the bishop's rail will be remembered for it, because nobody has to. You have a boiler that will not last the winter and a bishop who would like to see people kneel.
events.flavorPrompt: A restricted grant that is really a request, delivered by a finance officer with no tone.

choices.label: Take the grant and put in the rail
choices.outcome: The rail goes in before Lent, oak, with a gate. The bishop's name is not on it and everyone knows it is his. The people who kneel are glad. The people who do not kneel notice that they are now the ones making a statement, and some of them mind.

choices.label: Decline with thanks; the parish is not ready for it
choices.outcome: You write a careful paragraph about the parish's own pace. The finance officer thanks you for the prompt reply. The money goes to a parish two deaneries over, whose pastor is mentioned warmly at the next clergy day, and you understand that you have been mentioned too, less warmly, somewhere you were not.

choices.label: Ask whether the fund could stretch to the boiler, since the church must be warm to kneel in
choices.outcome: You make the case in person and he laughs, which you had not expected, and says the fund cannot but he can. A check for the boiler comes from somewhere else in the chancery. The rail does not go in. He does not ask about it again this year, and you both know that is a loan.

events.title: One Mass, Sung
events.body: At the deanery meeting {@bishop} talks for twenty minutes about music, which is longer than he talks about money, and the pastors who know him understand that this is the point of the meeting. He would like every parish of any size to have one Sunday Mass with the ordinary sung in Latin, chant, no guitars, the way the Council actually asked for and nobody did. He says it is not an instruction. He says he knows what music directors are like. He looks at you when he says it, or you think he does, and afterward, in the parking lot, the dean says he thinks the bishop meant you, because your parish is the size he was describing and your music director is exactly what he was describing. The dean says he is only passing it along.
events.flavorPrompt: A deanery meeting where the bishop talks about chant and looks at one pastor.

choices.label: Begin a sung Latin Mass at the early hour and find a schola
choices.outcome: The music director says she will not be part of it and you tell her she does not have to be. Six voices from the college come on Sundays. The seven o'clock grows. The bishop hears and sends a note with one line in it, which is more than he sends most men.

choices.label: Sing the Kyrie and the Agnus Dei in Latin at every Mass and leave the rest alone
choices.outcome: It is a small thing and the parish takes it as one. The music director grumbles and learns it. At the next deanery meeting the bishop says, to the room, that he has heard some parishes have begun, and you decide he means you, and this time you are probably right.

choices.label: Let it pass; the music director has been here twenty years and you have been here two
choices.outcome: You say nothing to anyone and the meeting goes into the folder of meetings. The bishop does not follow up, because he said it was not an instruction, and he does not forget, because it was one.

events.title: For the Sake of Unity
events.body: The vicar for clergy comes out himself, which means it is not his idea. He says {@bishop} has had letters about the Latin Mass at {parish}, not many, but from people who write well, and that the bishop's concern is not the Latin but the sorting: one Mass for one kind of Catholic and the rest for the others, and a parish that learns to think of itself in two halves. The bishop would like the Latin Mass to end, gently, before it becomes a cause. The vicar says the bishop is asking, and that he was told to say the word asking, and that you should hear it as a kindness that he is asking rather than the other thing. He says all this sitting in your office with his coat on, as if he might be leaving at any moment, and then he stays an hour.
events.flavorPrompt: A vicar for clergy delivering a bishop's request to end a Latin Mass, carefully calling it a request.

choices.label: End it, gently, with a month's notice and a homily about one parish
choices.outcome: You give the schola a month and the parish a homily and neither is enough. The people who came for it drive to the next diocese on Sundays now, and you know their names. The vicar for clergy tells the bishop it was done well, and the bishop, who notices who does things well, notices.

choices.label: Keep it, and write to the bishop that the parish is more united than the letters suggest
choices.outcome: You write it well, and it does not matter. He does not answer. The vicar for clergy, the next time you see him, is friendly in the way men are friendly when they have been told to be. The Latin Mass continues, and so does the file.

effects.value: Kept a Latin Mass the bishop asked to end

choices.label: Move it to a Wednesday evening, where it will trouble nobody's letters
choices.outcome: The Wednesday Mass is small and devout and the schola comes anyway. The Sunday schedule is one parish again, on paper. The vicar reports that the pastor found a way, which is the highest thing the chancery says about anyone.

events.title: Matching Funds
events.body: {@bishop} has an architect he likes and a fund he controls and a phrase, renewal of worship spaces, that he uses in every letter now. This one is addressed to you. The diocese will match, dollar for dollar up to sixty thousand, a parish project to bring the sanctuary of {parish} into line with the reformed liturgy: the high altar reduced or removed, the reredos gone, a freestanding altar of stone in the center of a space that opens toward the people. The architect will come at the diocese's expense. The letter observes that {parish} has the means, which is true, and the standing, which is flattering, and that its sanctuary is the last of its kind in the deanery, which is the sentence he wanted you to read twice. The building committee will have to be told. The building committee includes the grandson of the man who paid for the marble.
events.flavorPrompt: A bishop offering money to modernize a sanctuary he considers the last of its kind.

choices.label: Take the money and the architect and do it properly
choices.outcome: It takes two years and the parish's share is sixty thousand and the grandson resigns from the committee in a letter to the newspaper. The bishop comes to dedicate it and calls it the finest sanctuary in the diocese, and the architect photographs it, and the seven o'clock is half what it was.

choices.label: Decline: the parish loves its sanctuary and you will not be the man who took it out
choices.outcome: You write it plainly, and you add that you are grateful, and you are not. The architect goes elsewhere. The bishop's next letter to the deanery mentions the parishes that have begun renewal and does not mention yours, which is its own kind of mention.

choices.label: Accept the architect's study, and let the study take a long time
choices.outcome: The architect comes and measures and draws and the committee meets and asks for revisions and the revisions take a year. The diocese pays for the study. Nothing is built. The bishop, who has done this himself, knows exactly what you are doing, and lets you, for now.

events.title: Face to Face
events.body: The bishop's Lenten letter to the priests, which is usually about fasting, is this year about the sacrament of reconciliation and the option, provided for in the rite and, he says, too rarely provided for in the diocese, of confessing face to face. He would like every parish to offer it. He does not say every parish must build a room; he says he is aware that some churches have only the old boxes, and that he would be grateful if pastors would look at what could be done. The letter is warm. It is also, the dean points out, the third year running the bishop has asked, and the parishes that have not looked at what could be done are becoming a list.
events.flavorPrompt: A Lenten letter asking, for the third year, for reconciliation rooms.

choices.label: Build a reconciliation room beside the booths, and keep both
choices.outcome: The room takes a side aisle and twenty-two thousand dollars and is used, mostly, by people who would not have come to the box. The box keeps its line. The bishop's next letter names the parishes that have begun, and yours is among them, and the dean is glad to have one fewer name to explain.

choices.label: Write back that the boxes have a line out the door and the room would not
choices.outcome: It is true, and you say it kindly, and you offer face-to-face by appointment in the office, which you have always offered. The chancery thanks you for the letter. Your parish stays on the list, but the dean, who reads your letter, says it was a good one.

choices.label: Promise to look at what could be done, and then not look
choices.outcome: You write that the matter is under study. It is not. The dean knows it is not. Next Lent the letter comes again, and the list is a year longer, and you are still on it.

events.title: Not a Request
events.body: The letter is from {@bishop} and it is one paragraph. He writes that he has asked, and that he has been patient, and that he is now directing that the Sunday Masses at {parish} be celebrated facing the people, as is the practice of the diocese, effective the first Sunday of next month. He writes that he is aware of what the rubrics permit and that he is exercising the authority the rubrics give him to order the liturgy in his diocese. He writes that this is not a request. He writes that he expects a reply. There is no sympathy in it and no threat, and it is signed by hand. The chancellor has copied the file. You read it twice in the office and once in the church, standing where you stand at the seven o'clock, facing the way you face.
events.flavorPrompt: A one-paragraph letter from a bishop who has stopped asking.

choices.label: Comply, and tell the parish the bishop has spoken
choices.outcome: You say from the pulpit that the bishop has directed it and that a pastor who promised obedience keeps it, and you do not say what you think, and everyone can tell. The families who came for the seven o'clock stay a month and then find another parish. The bishop's reply to your reply is one line: thank you.

choices.label: Comply, and preach on obedience as if you meant it, because you do
choices.outcome: The homily is about the promise you made with your hands in his and about what it costs to keep a promise you would rather not, and it is the best you have preached in a year. The seven o'clock stays. The bishop reads it, because someone sends it to him, and something in the file changes.

choices.label: Refuse in writing, citing the rubrics, and keep the altar as it is
choices.outcome: You cite the General Instruction and you are right about what it says and it does not matter. The vicar general comes in person. The letter that follows his visit is not about the altar. Every pastor in the diocese knows your name by Easter, and the ones who admire you are not the ones who decide where you go next.

effects.value: Refused a written directive from the bishop

events.title: The Permission Is Withdrawn
events.body: The decree is two pages and has a protocol number, which is how you know it went through the chancellor and the canonist and possibly Rome. {@bishop} withdraws, effective in sixty days, the permission for the celebration of the older form of the Mass at {parish}, and cites the norms of 2021, and cites the good of the diocese, and cites nothing about you, which is the courtesy of a decree. The families who drive an hour for it will have nowhere in the diocese to go. There is a right of recourse and the decree says so, in the last paragraph, in the language of a document that expects not to be appealed. The vicar for clergy calls the same afternoon to say that the bishop hopes you will understand, and that he asked him to say that, and that he does hope it.
events.flavorPrompt: A decree withdrawing permission for the older Mass, and a phone call that hopes you understand.

choices.label: End it on the day, and drive with the families to the last one across the line
choices.outcome: The last Mass is full and quiet and afterward the families thank you as if you had done it for them, which you did. You go with them, once, to the parish two hours away, and sit in the back, and come home. The bishop's office notes that the decree was obeyed without incident.

choices.label: Ask for six months to wind it down and find the families a home
choices.outcome: He gives you four. It is enough to write to the pastor across the line and to say the goodbyes properly and not enough to make it painless. The chancery notes that you asked, and that you were granted it, and that you did not ask for more.

choices.label: Obey the decree and lodge recourse with Rome, publicly
choices.outcome: The Mass ends on the day because the decree is the decree. The recourse goes to Rome with a canonist's help and a press release you did not write but did not stop. Rome takes fourteen months and says the bishop was within his authority. By then everyone in the diocese knows which side you are on, including the men who decide where you go.

effects.value: Took a bishop to Rome over the older Mass

events.title: A Quieter Year
events.body: {@bishop} asks you to lunch, which is not a thing he does, and orders soup, and talks about the seminary for twenty minutes before he arrives at it. He has been reading you. Everyone has. He does not say you are wrong, and on two of the columns he says you were right. He says the diocese has one voice in public and it is his, and that when a priest of the diocese has a louder one the newspapers stop calling the chancery and start calling the priest, and that this has begun to happen. He would like a quieter year. He says it as a favor between men. He pays for lunch. You understand that a bishop who asks a favor at lunch is a bishop who has decided not to write a letter yet.
events.flavorPrompt: A bishop at lunch asking a priest, as a favor, to write less.

choices.label: Give him the quiet year
choices.outcome: You stop the column and decline the interviews and the podcast forgets you in a month. The people who read you feel abandoned and say so. The chancery notices that the phone has stopped ringing, and the bishop, at the next clergy day, shakes your hand a beat longer than the others.

choices.label: Keep writing, and send him every draft before it runs
choices.outcome: He reads them. He changes almost nothing and once, in the margin, writes good. The columns are more careful and nobody can say why. It is not the quiet year he asked for and it is not nothing, and he decides to take it as something.

choices.label: Keep writing; he did not make it an order and you did not make it a promise
choices.outcome: The next column runs on schedule. The one after it is about bishops. You did not mean it to be, exactly. The lunch is not repeated, and the letter he had decided not to write yet is written.

effects.value: Kept writing after the bishop asked for a quiet year

events.title: As a Favor
events.body: The bishop's secretary calls to say {@bishop} would like a word, and the word, when it comes, is a job: the deanery's finances are a mess, three parishes have not filed in two years, and he would like someone he trusts to go through the books and tell him what is true before the auditors tell him what is wrong. It is not a chancery post. It carries no title and no stipend and something like four hours a week for the better part of a year. He says he asked because you can count and because you can keep your mouth shut, and that he does not say that about many men. He says it is a favor. He does not say what a favor from a bishop is worth, and you have been ordained long enough to have a guess.
events.flavorPrompt: A bishop asking a priest to quietly audit a deanery, as a favor with no title.

choices.label: Do it, and do it well, and say nothing about it to anyone
choices.outcome: It takes eleven months and you find what he was afraid of at one parish and better than he hoped at the other two. He reads the report twice. He does not thank you in public, because the point was that nobody would know, and he does not forget.

choices.label: Decline; the parish has all of you and you told them it would
choices.outcome: He takes it well, which is worse than the alternative. Someone else does it. You hear later that the someone else is a classmate of yours, and that the bishop has begun to say the classmate can count.

choices.label: Do it, and before you leave the room, tell him which parish you would like someday
choices.outcome: He laughs, and then he does not, and he writes something down. You do the work and it is good. Whether the thing he wrote down was the parish or the fact that you asked, you will not know for years.

events.title: A Room in the Rectory
events.body: {@bishop} asks whether you have a room. A priest of the diocese is coming home from six months of treatment for drinking, and the bishop would like him to live somewhere steady for a year, with a pastor who will eat dinner with him and notice if he stops coming down to dinner. He will help at Masses. He will not be given a parish for a while. The bishop says he chose you because your rectory is quiet and because you do not gossip, and because the last two men he asked said no, which he mentions without any weight on it at all. It is a request. He says so. He also says that he will remember it either way, and that he means that kindly, and you believe he does.

choices.label: Yes; there is a room, and dinner is at six
choices.outcome: He moves in with two suitcases and a breviary and is, for a year, the best-prepared homilist in the deanery. There are two bad weeks in the winter and you notice them, which was the job. The bishop comes to dinner once, unannounced, and says nothing about why.

choices.label: Yes, with conditions: no keys to the sacristy safe, and the vicar for clergy calls monthly
choices.outcome: The bishop agrees to the conditions at once, which tells you he had expected worse ones. The year goes well enough. The man knows about the conditions, because men in recovery always know, and does not hold them against you, quite.

choices.label: No; not this year, not with what the parish is carrying
choices.outcome: He says he understands and asks the next man on his list. You hear who took him in. It is a pastor you had thought less of, and you think of him differently now, and so does the bishop.
